question: How are heavy and superheavy nuclei formed?
intro: My research develops computational models of heavy-ion reactions to understand and predict the formation of heavy and superheavy nuclei. Stochastic simulation, uncertainty quantification and scientific computing provide the principal methods for this work.

areas.title: Nuclear Reaction Dynamics
areas.text: Langevin-based stochastic modelling of heavy-ion reactions. Fusion–evaporation reactions and the synthesis of superheavy elements are applications of the same description, with predictions for Z = 119 and Z = 120 made with KEWPIE3. Current work revisits the fusion dynamics in the fusion-by-diffusion model for fusion–evaporation production cross sections.

areas.title: Uncertainty Quantification
areas.text: Bayesian optimisation and machine learning applied to estimate nuclear model parameters and their uncertainties, with systematic benchmarking of competing models.

current.title: KEWPIE3 development and validation
paragraphs: **Objective:** validate and publish KEWPIE3, the refinement of the KEWPIE2 cascade code (which describes the survival of the excited nucleus) with an implemented and calibrated formation step, for fusion-evaporation cross-section predictions in superheavy element synthesis.
**Key question:** how can the calculation of the compound nucleus formation probability be improved with Langevin-based stochastic approaches?

current.title: Uncertainty analysis of nuclear reaction models
paragraphs: **Objective:** constrain the compound nucleus formation probability in superheavy element synthesis through systematic uncertainty analysis.

previous.summary_title: Study of Reaction Mechanisms for the Synthesis of Superheavy Elements
previous.meta: PhD thesis, University of Caen Normandy (2024)
previous.summary: This thesis investigates the synthesis of super-heavy elements (Z ≥ 104) by fusion–evaporation reactions. These nuclei do not exist in nature because their macroscopic fission barriers vanish, and they are stabilised by quantum shell correction. The work improves the predictive power of the Kewpie2 model, with fusion–evaporation described in three stages (capture, formation and survival), by implementing the formation step in the code, the basis of KEWPIE3.
key_results: **Formation step implemented** in the Kewpie2 code for the first time, using both the overdamped and the full Langevin formalisms.
**Injection-point distance** optimised on cold and hot fusion datasets. Evaporation residue cross sections for hot fusion are reproduced, typically with accuracy better than an order of magnitude.

**Cold fusion:** multiple neutron emission channels are explained by an additional structural term. The 1n channel deviates from the data by a factor, while the 2n and 3n channels are within an order of magnitude.

**Survival probability** modelled with the latest data for superheavy elements. The formation and survival steps are tested extensively and compared with the Fusion-by-Diffusion model for sets of 27 cold and 24 hot fusion reactions.

**Friction:** analysis of the reduced friction coefficients in the overdamped approach suggests that the dynamics is not fully damped, so a full one-dimensional Langevin formalism is implemented and applied to hot fusion data. Model predictions are within an order of magnitude of the data.
**Predictions** for the synthesis of elements with Z = 119 and 120 align with results from other codes.
**New method** proposed for studying ratios of formation probabilities for the synthesis of ^258^No and ^259^Db.
**Conclusion:** the work makes the code a self-contained tool for studying superheavy-element synthesis and guiding future experiments.

previous.summary_title: Nuclear Structure Studies with Symmetry Conserving Configuration Mixing Methods
previous.meta: MSc dissertation, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid · Erasmus Mundus Joint Master in Nuclear Physics · September 2020 · Supervisor: Dr. Tomás Raúl Rodríguez Frutos
previous.summary: This dissertation describes the general framework of the symmetry conserving configuration mixing (SCCM) method, a beyond-mean-field approach based on the variational principle, and applies an axially symmetric version of it to study the structure of the even-even argon isotopes (A = 32 to 58). The same method is then used to explore the structure of ^152,154^Nd and ^78^Kr. The argon isotope study was carried out with T. R. Rodríguez Frutos and is available as a preprint on HAL.
key_results: **Argon isotopes:** they exhibit collectivity with mixing of oblate and prolate shapes.
**Magic numbers** N = 20 and 28 persist along the isotopic chain, shown by higher first excitation energies than in the neighbouring isotopes.
**Neutron sub-shell closures** (2p1/2 and pf-shell) at ^56^Ar and ^58^Ar are indicated by the first excitation energies and the nuclear charge radius.
**Binding energy per nucleon and charge radii** are reproduced along the isotopic chain, and the axial GCM-SCCM results show good agreement with the experimental data.
**^152,154^Nd** are found to be well deformed, with two distinct rotational bands: prolate and oblate shapes coexist.

**^78^Kr** shows an admixture of oblate and prolate shapes. The moment of inertia of the first excited 0^+^ state is about one third of that of the ground state, which reinforces the shape coexistence.
